name: Hydroxyapatite (toothpaste)

lead: Hydroxyapatite toothpaste uses the same mineral that makes up tooth enamel, in tiny particles, as a fluoride-free way to protect and remineralise teeth. People switch to it for smoother enamel and brighter, healthier-looking teeth.

The particles are meant to deposit on enamel and fill microscopic defects in demineralised areas, supported by saliva's calcium and phosphate. An 18-month adult trial found it not inferior to fluoride at preventing new cavities, and a child trial and small sensitivity trials have also been positive. In bleaching trials it reduced sensitivity when added to peroxide; evidence that it whitens teeth by itself was not found.

paras: It replaces regular toothpaste in the twice-daily brushing routine, often used by people avoiding fluoride or managing sensitivity, and alongside whitening treatments.

Trials report no safety concerns, and the main safety debate in the field concerns fluoride rather than hydroxyapatite. Long-term, large-scale data are still limited, and fluoride remains the long-established standard for cavity prevention.

angle.text: Hydroxyapatite toothpaste deposits enamel-like mineral on teeth, remineralising and smoothing enamel so teeth look brighter and healthier. It is used as a fluoride-free option, and an 18-month adult trial found it matched fluoride for cavity prevention; whitening on its own has not been shown.

lead: Hydroxyapatite toothpaste contains synthetic hydroxyapatite, a calcium phosphate mineral that is also the main mineral of tooth enamel, in micro- or nano-sized crystals. It is marketed as a fluoride-free alternative for protecting and remineralising enamel [1]. Review authors describe how the particles deposit on and restore demineralised enamel surfaces, and they are being explored as an anti-caries agent without fluoride [1].

Interest in it connects to appearance through tooth health, enamel erosion, sensitivity and whitening: trials have examined it for dentin hypersensitivity, for reducing sensitivity during bleaching, and for erosive enamel lesions.

An 18-month randomized trial in adults found a fluoride-free hydroxyapatite toothpaste not inferior to a 1450 ppm fluoride toothpaste for preventing new caries [2], and a 24-month trial in children reported results favouring hydroxyapatite-fluoride toothpastes on active enamel lesions [3]. Fluoride remains the long-established standard in caries prevention.
infobox: Enamel remineralisation, caries prevention, sensitivity relief [1]

paras: Tooth enamel is largely hydroxyapatite. Once formed, it cannot be biologically repaired by the body, and saliva supplies calcium, phosphate and fluoride ions that support remineralisation of demineralised surfaces. Hydroxyapatite toothpastes add particles intended to deposit directly on enamel and fill in lesions, a mechanism examined in laboratory, in situ and clinical studies [1]. Nano-hydroxyapatite is also studied outside dentistry as a bone graft and scaffold material, a separate field [4].

Caries prevention. An 18-month double-blind trial of 189 adults compared a fluoride-free hydroxyapatite toothpaste with 1450 ppm fluoride toothpaste; 89.3% of the hydroxyapatite group and 87.4% of the fluoride group showed no increase in DMFS, and the authors concluded non-inferiority [2]. A triple-blind trial in 610 young children tested hydroxyapatite-fluoride toothpastes against fluoride toothpastes over 24 months and reported a statistically significant reduction in enamel lesions in the hydroxyapatite-fluoride group [3]. A scoping review of nano-hydroxyapatite in early caries mapped the literature on remineralisation of early lesions, and a narrative review summarised in vitro, in situ and in vivo findings [1].

Sensitivity and whitening. A double-blind randomized trial of 105 people found a fluoride-free nano-hydroxyapatite gel toothpaste produced lower dentin hypersensitivity scores at 2 and 4 weeks than fluoride or placebo. In a 60-person bleaching trial, 6% hydrogen peroxide with 2% nano-hydroxyapatite produced comparable shade change to peroxide alone, with significantly less sensitivity; shade partly relapsed by 9 months in both groups. Other trials examined it with ozone on early approximal caries  and on erosive lesions caused by orange juice. Evidence that hydroxyapatite toothpaste whitens teeth on its own is not found in these sources.

Fluoride is described as a cornerstone of caries prevention through enamel remineralisation, inhibition of demineralisation and antibacterial activity, although controversies persist over systemic exposure and community water fluoridation. Hydroxyapatite toothpaste is presented by reviewers as a fluoride-free option under investigation, and trials so far have mostly compared it with fluoride products rather than with no treatment [1][2]. Longer trials in more diverse populations are not found in the sources reviewed.

The cited trials report it as safe and well tolerated; the authors of the adult trial concluded it was a safe and efficient anticaries agent [2]. Regulatory status of specific products varies by country and is not addressed in the cited studies.

timeline.event: Trial of bleaching with and without nano-hydroxyapatite reports reduced sensitivity.
